# **Introduction** 

We are building a machine learning model that helps Banca Massiccia (“the bank”) to better predict loan applicant’s probability of default (PD). We are utilizing company financial statement data to build features and using their default history to build labels. We included three algorithms – Logistic Regression, LightGBM, and Generalized Additive Model (GAM), compared their performances and conducted calibration. Using walk-forward analysis as our main evaluation method, we found that LightGBM outperforms the other two algorithms.

## **Structure of this Report** 

This project update report summarizes our work into primarily three parts. Data preparation details how we processed raw bank statement data including data splitting into training, validation and test sets, anomaly checks, missing value handling and imputation, and how we defined and transformed the features. Modeling introduces model selection, model training, and model evaluation. Last but not least, we discuss our calibration methods and the adjustments we made.

## **Data Preprocessing**

### **Data Splitting: the Walk-forward Analysis [yl14490@nyu.edu](mailto:yl14490@nyu.edu)**

Data splitting is done before any of our data imputation, because we expected to use median-based imputation methods, and imputing the data before the train-test split introduces target leakage – the imputed data would contain information from the test set. 

We decided to use the walk-forward method for model evaluation, and therefore, the full data set is split according to the logic of walk-forward. Specifically in each round, we have a training set, a validation set, and a test set. The validation set is primarily used for hyperparameter tuning and preventing overfitting. Within each round, the validation set is about 25% the size of the training set, and the samples in the validation set are drawn randomly from the samples set aside for training. We also made sure that the after-split training set cannot see anything from the validation set, which is a standard technique to prevent leakage. 

Below is an illustration of our walk-forward process:

| Round | Train (80% of IDs) | Validation (20% of IDs) | Test |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| **1** | companies defaulted between 2008.6 \- 2009.5 or haven’t defaulted at 2009.5 but `stmt_date` \= 2007.12.31 | A sample of `id`s from the non-test set that defaulted between 2008.6 \- 2009.5 | companies defaulted between 2009.6 \- 2010.5 or haven’t defaulted at 2010.5 but `stmt_date` ≤ 2008.12.31 |
| **2** | companies defaulted between 2008.6 \- 2010.5 or haven’t defaulted at 2010.5 but `stmt_date` ≤ 2008.12.31 | `id`s from the non-test set that defaulted between 2008.6 \- 2010.5 | companies defaulted between 2010.6 \- 2011.5 or haven’t defaulted at 2011.5 but `stmt_date` ≤ 2009.12.31 |
| **3** | companies defaulted between 2008.6 \- 2011.5 or haven’t defaulted at 2011.5 but `stmt_date` ≤ 2009.12.31 | `id`s from the non-test set that defaulted between 2008.6 \- 2011.5 | companies defaulted between 2011.6 \- 2012.5 or haven’t defaulted at 2012.5 but `stmt_date` ≤ 2010.12.31 |
| **4** | companies defaulted between 2008.6 \- 2012.5 or haven’t defaulted at 2012.5 but `stmt_date` ≤ 2010.12.31 | `id`s from the non-test set that defaulted between 2008.6 \- 2012.5 | companies defaulted between 2012.6 \- 2013.5 or haven’t defaulted at 2013.5 but `stmt_date` ≤ 2011.12.31 |

Table 2.1

We split the data accordingly into 4 groups of train, validation, and test sets. In each training round, the model will not be able to see any data from future rounds. 

### **Anomaly Check [cp4516@nyu.edu](mailto:cp4516@nyu.edu)**

We checked the features in financial statements whether they violate accounting rules. Two types of issues are flagged(with the original values kept) and will be used as features:

| Flags | Anomaly | Rows | Default rate |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| neg\_bs\_flag | Any of 14 asset and liability columns\* is negative. | 6662 | 5.34% |
| neg\_pl\_flag | Operating revenues, COGS, or financing expenses is negative, or implied depreciation( ebitda \- prof\_operations) is negative. | 10508 | 6.60%  |

Table 2.2  
\*These 14 columns are: asst\_intang\_fixed, asst\_tang\_fixed, asst\_fixed\_fin, AR, liab\_lt, liab\_lt\_emp, debt\_bank\_st/lt, debt\_fin\_st/lt, AP\_st/lt, debt\_st, debt\_lt  
We created the flags instead of deleting or adjusting these columns since the affected rows default more often than average(4.37%), deleting them might lose information.  
Some other anomalies were also found but not addressed, such as rounding noise(identity gaps under 1% of total assets).

### **Missing Values [yl14490@nyu.edu](mailto:yl14490@nyu.edu)**

We found that out of all variables from the raw dataset, six variables have a ratio of missing values larger than 10% (as shown in Table 2.3). Note that eqty\_corp\_family\_tot is completely missing, therefore, we didn’t use this variable at all in any feature. Missing def\_date isn’t a warning because it simply means the company hasn’t defaulted in this period. So we only focused on days\_rec, debt\_fin\_st, debt\_bank\_st, and AP\_st. 

![][image1]  
Table 2.3

Regarding these four variables, we didn’t blindly impute all of them by replacing them with zeros, means or medians (Bryzgalova et al., 2025\) across the entire training dataset, because financial data have complex and systematic missingness patterns. Instead, we used a two-step process to preserve the authentic information from the raw data: first, we constructed binary flag features as an indication of missing values. Second, we proceeded to impute the missing values using a cross-sectional method using ateco\_sector. For example, if a company’s debt\_fin\_st is “null”, we fill it with the median of the sector the company is in. 

Similarly, since we had expected to build a lot of financial ratios as features and we wanted to avoid having “inf” in the feature data set, we checked the number of zeros for all the variables in the raw data set. As shown in Table 2.4, there are five variables with more than 10% of zero values. To handle this, we also created a series of binary zero flags, and we proceeded to convert the ratios with zero numerators to “nan”. This combined with zero flags will provide a better picture to the model that this value is not missing but an undefined fraction.

Table 2.4 

### **Feature Aggregation [yl14490@nyu.edu](mailto:yl14490@nyu.edu)**

Since our data is essentially a panel data set, and that we intend to preserve only one row of data for each company in each round of the training data, we need to aggregate multiple years (and multiple rows) of company data into one. Following Kim et al. (2021), we implemented a decaying weighted sum of features. For example, assuming we have 3 years of data for a company, for the feature “Short-term debt share” (STDS) we aggregate in the following way:

${STDSAVG}_{t}=\frac{1-{\varphi }^{}}{1-{\varphi }^{3}}({STDS}_{t}+\varphi {STDS}_{t-1}+{\varphi }^{2}{STDS}_{t-2}),$ where $\varphi =\frac{1}{2}$

The normalization term $\frac{1-{\varphi }^{}}{1-{\varphi }^{3}}$ makes sure the weights sum to 1, and $\varphi =\frac{1}{2}$ means that the weights halve every year. Accordingly, ${STDSAVG}_{t}$ is the aggregated information from previous years of the borrower. This encodes time-series information in an intuitive way that we would expect information from further in the past should matter less than more recent information. 

## **Variables: Labels and Features**

### **Dependent Variable \- Label** [cp4516@nyu.edu](mailto:cp4516@nyu.edu)

We define the dependent variable as a **binary indicator**. The dependent variable equals 1 if the firm defaults during the prediction period, otherwise 0\.  
For prediction period, we decided to set the potential delay of financial statements published at **5 months**, which is based on 2 relevant documents:

1. Italian civil law: Art. 2364 (Codice Civile, n.d., art. 2364\) requires shareholder approval of the financial statements within 120 days of year-end (April 30), and Art. 2435 requires filing with the Registro delle Imprese within 30 days of approval. The deadline is therefore May 30\.  
2. Moody’s practice report: Moody's KMV (2004, p. 16\) states that "most private firm statements are not available to lenders until three or four months after the statement date."

### **Collinearity Check**

We haven't implemented this part yet, so the following is our expected steps.

1. To prevent data leakage, we will only use the training data from the first round of walk-forward process(stmt\_date \= 2007.12.31 in this case).  
2. Calculate the VIF values for all the features.  
3. For those features with VIF \> 10, excluding the one with lowest single-feature AUC.  
4. Repeat steps 2 and 3 until all the VIF are lower than 10\.   
5. Keep the final feature list and use it in every walk-forward round.

\*Since we will try tree models and linear models like logistic regression, and collinearity check will only be performed for linear models, the features used in the two types of models will differ slightly.

### **Feature standardization**

We haven't implemented this part yet, so the following is our expected steps.  
For linear models, each continuous feature is standardized to z \= (x − μ) / σ, dummy variables and flags are not scaled. In every round, μ and σ are computed from that round's training data only and then applied to the validation and test data.

# **Modeling**

We used primarily three models for the training process: logistic regression with weight of evidence (WoE), LightGBM, and Generalized Additive models with an Explainable Boosting Machine.

# **Calibration [kn2827@nyu.edu](mailto:kn2827@nyu.edu)**

- [ ] How do our models perform in terms of calibration  
- [x] ~~What calibration methods are used and **why**~~

In each walk-forward round with test year T, we first tune the hyperparameters and retrain the model on the full training data (2007 to T−1) using the best ones. We then calibrate the model on that same training data.

1. Score the training data with the refit model and sort by score, worst first. Split it into k equal buckets of N/k companies each.   
2. Calculate the real default rate in each bucket.  
3. Fit a curve that maps quantiles to default rates.  
4. Transform the mapped PD from step 3 into a PD for the real population:  
   ${p}_{i}^{*}=\ {\pi }_{T}\times \frac{{p}_{i}\ -\ {p}_{i}\ {\pi }_{S}}{{\pi }_{S}\ -\ {p}_{i}\ {\pi }_{S}\ +\ {p}_{i}\ {\pi }_{T}\ -\ {\pi }_{S}{\pi }_{T}}{\ }$

   where  
   1. ${\pi }_{S}$:  overall default rate of the training data  
   2. ${\pi }_{T}$:  true population default rate  
   3. ${p}_{i}$:  mapped PD of observation i  
   4. ${p}_{i}^{*}$:  calibrated PD for observation i  
5. Score the test year T with the refit model then apply the step 4 mapping and transformation to get the calibrated PD.
